title: Upper GI Disorders: GERD, Peptic Ulcer Disease & Acute Bleeding
html:
Upper gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms range from common reflux to life-threatening bleeding or perforation. The RN should not treat every epigastric complaint as simple indigestion: dysphagia, weight loss, blood loss, sudden severe pain, and circulatory changes redirect care toward urgent assessment. In suspected bleeding, airway and perfusion take priority over finding the exact lesion.

Learning goals

  • Identify GERD alarm features that need evaluation rather than routine self-treatment.
  • Explain common peptic-ulcer causes and prevention of recurrence.
  • Recognize upper GI bleeding, shock, perforation, and rebleeding.
  • Coordinate safe resuscitation, endoscopy preparation, and postprocedure monitoring.
  • Teach H. pylori treatment adherence and documented eradication testing.

GERD: distinguish typical symptoms from red flags

Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) occurs when gastric contents repeatedly reflux into the esophagus, causing symptoms or injury. Typical symptoms include heartburn and regurgitation. Ask about timing, food and position triggers, nighttime symptoms, prescribed and over-the-counter medicines, and effect on eating or sleep. Avoid assuming chest discomfort is reflux until potentially serious cardiac causes are assessed. New or progressive dysphagia, painful swallowing, unintentional weight loss, vomiting, anemia, or GI bleeding needs clinician evaluation and often upper endoscopy rather than indefinite empiric acid suppression. For uncomplicated symptoms, teach the individualized plan: take prescribed acid-suppressing medicine correctly, avoid personally identified triggers, consider weight management when relevant, and avoid lying down soon after meals. Do not present restrictive diets as a substitute for evaluation of alarm symptoms.

Peptic ulcer disease: treat the cause

A peptic ulcer is a mucosal break in the stomach or duodenum. Helicobacter pylori infection and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), including over-the-counter ibuprofen or naproxen, are major causes. Antiplatelets, anticoagulants, and other medicines may increase bleeding risk, especially in combination; review all medicines and prior ulcer or bleed history without independently stopping essential therapy. Epigastric discomfort, nausea, early satiety, or no symptoms at all can precede a complication. Perforation can cause sudden severe abdominal pain, a rigid abdomen, and signs of peritonitis or shock. Bleeding can cause hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis, melena, dizziness, syncope, or a rapid pulse. A client can deteriorate even before hemoglobin reflects the full acute blood loss.

Prescribed proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs) help ulcer healing and are used in many upper GI bleeding pathways. If H. pylori is confirmed, use the current prescribed eradication regimen; antibiotic resistance and prior exposure affect selection, so do not recommend an old one-size-fits-all combination. Reinforce completing every dose and managing side effects with the care team. Eradication must be confirmed with an appropriate breath, stool, or biopsy-based test after therapy. Current ACG guidance calls for testing at least four weeks after antibiotics and withholding PPIs or potassium-competitive acid blockers for at least two weeks before testing when directed, to avoid a false-negative result. The clinician should give a safe interim acid-control plan; the RN should not tell a client to stop a necessary medicine without that plan.

Upper GI bleeding: stabilize before the scope

Upper GI bleeding may arise from an ulcer, erosive disease, esophageal lesion, or varices; the management pathway differs by cause. Assess airway protection, mental status, respiratory status, orthostatic symptoms, blood pressure, pulse, perfusion, skin, urine output, emesis, and stool. Bright red hematemesis suggests active bleeding; coffee-ground emesis or melena can represent older blood, but neither guarantees safety. A brisk upper source can also produce red stool. Review NSAIDs, aspirin, anticoagulants, liver disease, and prior bleeding. Obtain ordered IV access, blood count, chemistry, coagulation studies, type and crossmatch, and serial values. Keep the client NPO as ordered, support prescribed fluids and blood products, and observe closely for aspiration and worsening shock. A single normal early hemoglobin must not override tachycardia, hypotension, syncope, or ongoing blood loss.

After initial stabilization, upper endoscopy identifies and may treat the source. For many hospitalized upper GI bleeding clients, guideline-based care includes endoscopy within about 24 hours; unstable clients need immediate resuscitation and individualized urgent decisions first. Prepare consent and medication review per policy; verify anticoagulant or antiplatelet management with the treating team rather than making an independent hold or restart decision. After endoscopic therapy, monitor for recurrent hematemesis or melena, rising pulse, falling pressure, reduced urine output, new pain, and serial laboratory change. Follow the ordered PPI and transfusion plan; transfusion thresholds vary with clinical context and active instability, so no single number replaces bedside reassessment. Rebleeding may need repeat endoscopic or other intervention.

Recognize perforation and procedure complications

Sudden severe abdominal pain with guarding or rigidity, fever, tachycardia, or shock after known ulcer disease raises concern for perforation and peritonitis. Escalate immediately, keep the client NPO, reassess airway and circulation, and prepare for ordered imaging, antibiotics, surgical evaluation, and fluid support. After endoscopy, new severe chest or abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fever, subcutaneous swelling, or respiratory distress also warrants urgent evaluation rather than being labeled routine postprocedure discomfort. Maintain aspiration precautions until the client is alert and the care team clears oral intake.

Plan discharge around recurrence prevention

Before discharge, confirm the specific bleeding source and treatment plan, medicine list, whether NSAIDs should be avoided or modified, and who will manage essential antithrombotic medicines. Teach the client to seek emergency care for vomiting blood, black stools with weakness, fainting, or sudden severe abdominal pain. If H. pylori was treated, document the test-of-cure order and timing rather than assuming symptoms prove eradication. Use teach-back for PPI timing, antibiotic completion, follow-up appointments, and what to do if bleeding symptoms return.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Note emesis and stool appearance, dysphagia, pain pattern, vital-sign trends, mentation, perfusion, urine output, medicine exposures, and prior GI history.
  2. Analyze cues: Distinguish uncomplicated reflux from alarm symptoms; consider ulcer, active bleeding, perforation, and possible variceal disease.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Airway compromise, hemorrhagic shock, perforation, and recurrent bleeding require immediate action.
  4. Generate solutions: Support ordered access, laboratory work, resuscitation, NPO status, cause-specific medicine, and endoscopy or surgical evaluation.
  5. Take action: Escalate deterioration promptly, monitor serial response, coordinate safe procedure preparation, and document blood loss without delaying stabilization.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Confirm stable perfusion, no recurrent bleeding, adequate urine output, recovery after intervention, and a clear ulcer-cause and follow-up plan.

Clinical example

A client who has taken frequent ibuprofen reports black stools, weakness, and near-syncope. Their heart rate rises and blood pressure falls, but the first hemoglobin is near baseline. The RN treats the vital signs and symptoms as possible significant upper GI blood loss, calls for urgent assessment, supports IV access and ordered resuscitation, prepares type and crossmatch and endoscopy, and reassesses airway, perfusion, stool, and serial results. Once stable, the team evaluates for ulcer disease, H. pylori, and a safer pain-management plan.
